Chapter 5: Harnessing Social and Environmental Influences for Lasting Change
So, here’s something a lot of us overlook—motivation and ability are important, sure, but they’re just part of the story. The people around you, and even the spaces you spend time in, can shape your habits way more than you might think. Sometimes these influences help you grow, but other times, they quietly hold you back.
Let’s dive into social motivation and ability—basically, the power people have over us. We’re wired to care about what others think. Friends, family, coworkers… even those casual acquaintances can nudge us for better or worse.
Just imagine you’re trying to get more exercise. It’s so much easier when a friend invites you to join a walking group, right? But what if you’re trying to quit smoking, and your coworkers keep heading out for smoke breaks? That’s tough.
Now, social ability takes it up a notch. This is all about others giving you real, practical support. Maybe it’s a mentor showing you the ropes, a partner picking up extra chores so you have time for a class, or a coworker covering your shift. These moments of help can make all the difference.
So, how can you put social influences to work for you? First, recruit allies—find those people who genuinely want to see you succeed and who’ll cheer you on or keep you accountable. Next, set clear expectations. When you share your goals out loud, it gives others a chance to support you in the right ways. And don’t be afraid to avoid negative influences—if someone’s always dragging you off track, maybe spend a little less time with them, at least while you’re building new habits.
When you shape your social circle with intention, you create a team that makes sticking with new behaviors so much easier.
But people aren’t the whole picture. The environment matters too—that’s where structural motivation and ability come in. Think of structural motivation as the built-in rewards and incentives you get throughout your day. Structural ability is all about the tools, systems, and physical setups that either help or hinder you.
Let’s say you want to eat healthier. If you put fruits and veggies right up front in your kitchen, and stash the junk food out of sight, you’re setting yourself up to make better choices without having to think so hard. Or maybe you’re trying to save more money—you could set up automatic transfers so saving just happens, no willpower required.
Want a few ways to tweak your environment?
Try adding small rewards for yourself when you stick to your new habits. Remove temptations, making those old habits just a little less convenient. Or, redesign your routines—maybe move things around or change the order of activities so it’s easier to do what you want to do.
These little changes can be surprisingly powerful, giving you that extra edge to stick with what matters most.
Here’s where things get really interesting—social and structural influences often work best together. Picture a workplace wellness program. Maybe there’s peer support, expert coaching, cash rewards, and even a gym on-site. All those pieces team up to make healthy habits a lot more likely to stick.
The big idea here? Don’t go it alone. Approach change as a team effort, using both your social network and your environment to back you up. When you bring your people, your spaces, and your own motivation together, you build a system that’s way more likely to deliver lasting results.
So, if there’s one thing to remember, it’s this—lasting change is rarely a solo act. By tapping into the power of your social circle and designing your environments with intention, you can make new behaviors not just possible, but sustainable.
